findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax such as `HEAD; <command>`, `exec()` evaluates it with the Node process's privileges. The replaced `execFile()` call safely passed `branch` as one argument; retain argument-separated execution.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve cancellation of the Git child process
findings.body: `exec()` returns the shell child rather than reliably exposing the `git` process it launches. Killing that returned child can leave `git show` or other descendants running and holding stdio, whereas `execFile()` returned the directly spawned Git child.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve cancellation of the actual Git process
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than necessarily returning `git`. On platforms where the shell forks `git`—notably Windows—calling `.kill()` on the returned `ChildProcess` can terminate only the shell while `git show` continues running and keeps its stdio open. Consumers can no longer reliably cancel expensive operations, unlike with the previous direct `execFile()` child.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body:
`exec()` interprets `branch` as shell syntax. Any caller-controlled value such as `main; rm -rf ...` or `$(command)` executes arbitrary commands with the process’s privileges; the previous `execFile()` call passed it safely as one argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch argument without invoking a shell
findings.body:
`exec()` interpolates `branch` into a shell command, enabling arbitrary command execution whenever callers supply untrusted input. For example, on POSIX, `showBranch("HEAD; touch /tmp/pwned")` executes `touch` with the Node process’s privileges. The previous `execFile()` implementation treated the branch as a single argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Avoid spawning unowned processes through branch interpolation
findings.body:
`exec` passes `branch` through a shell. An input such as `HEAD; yes >/dev/null &` starts a persistent background process outside the returned child’s ownership, so `.kill()` cannot reliably clean it up. Repeated calls with attacker-controlled or malformed branch values can exhaust CPU/process resources; even normal cancellation now targets the shell rather than reliably terminating Git.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
